uncited: *   **Inputs:** Reference projection images (Ground Truth) acquired at various rotation angles; initial scene parameters $\pi$ including rotation angle and volume data $\sigma$; optimization hyperparameters ($N_{rot}, N_{iter}, LR, \beta_1, \beta_2, \epsilon$).
*   **Voxel Grid:** A 3D grid representation of the object.
*   **Absorption Coefficient ($\sigma$):** A scalar value per voxel.
Value 1 means fully absorbing; 0 means no absorption.
*   **Update Buffer ($\sigma_{update}$):** A non-absorbing matrix (volume data) used to update the scene parameters.
*   $\pi_0$ is the absorption coefficient matrix of the volumetric object.
*   $f(x, y; \pi)$ is the rendering function mapping scene parameters to image coordinates.
*   $I_i$ is the pixel value in the rendered image.
**Initialize:** Set $N_{rot}$ (number of 45° rotations) and $N_{iter}$ (iterations per rotation).
*   **High GPU Memory Usage:** Auto-differential volume rendering requires significant GPU memory.
High resolutions or sample counts cause out-of-memory errors.
*   **Time Complexity:** The method is iterative and computationally expensive.
This limits the feasible resolution and sample count.

*   **When to Use:** Suitable for proof-of-concept demonstrations, small-scale volumetric reconstruction where high precision is not critical, or when traditional reconstruction methods fail due to complex lighting/material interactions that can be modeled in a differentiable renderer.
*   **When Not to Use:** For large-scale clinical CT scans requiring high resolution and speed; when GPU memory is constrained; when reference images are extremely noisy.
It builds upon the work of Zhao et al. [ZJL20] for mathematical insights into differentiable volume rendering and Hochhauser et al. [Hoc22] for X-ray spectrum rendering.
